title: India Within Striking Distance of 8% Growth, Says PMO's Shaktikanta Das
excerpt: The former RBI governor credited a decade of reforms — GST, banking clean-up, inflation targeting, digital payments — for 7.8% June-quarter growth, and named AI the next productivity frontier.
body:
• Shaktikanta Das, principal secretary to the prime minister and former RBI governor, said Sunday the Indian economy is "within striking distance of 8% growth" — after 7.8% growth in the June quarter and 7.9% last financial year.
  • Speaking at the Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi, Das credited a decade of reforms — GST, banking clean-up, flexible inflation targeting, digital payments and fiscal prudence — for building "strategic buffers" that let the economy absorb shocks.
  • He flagged AI as the next productivity frontier — for public service delivery, scientific discovery, healthcare and education — and called for deepening the corporate bond market, pension and insurance funds, and municipal finance.
  • What it means for you: the domestic-demand growth story underpins the investment case for India — with steady inward remittances and a services-trade surplus cited as pillars, the macro backdrop for NRI portfolios and repatriated savings remains supportive.

The Indian economy is within striking distance of 8% growth, a top official in the Prime Minister's Office said on Sunday, arguing that a decade of reforms has built the buffers that let India absorb global shocks and recover rapidly.

The case for 8%

"Many of the reforms undertaken over the past decade were not designed as one-off measures, but as strategic buffers to enable the economy to absorb disruptions and recover rapidly," principal secretary to the prime minister Shaktikanta Das said at the Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi. The former RBI governor pointed to the numbers: the economy expanded 7.8% in the June quarter after 7.9% growth last financial year, driven by strong domestic demand and investment.

Das listed the pillars: GST and banking reforms, flexible inflation targeting, the digital payments stack, and fiscal prudence. "India's resilience is not accidental. It is the outcome of broad and mutually reinforcing reforms," he said. On the external front, he said India's financial sector and prudent management had emerged as strong pillars of growth — with export diversification, free trade agreements, a sustained surplus in services trade and steady inward remittances keeping external indicators broadly resilient.

The road ahead: AI and deeper capital markets

Das said the pace of activity will accelerate over the next five years, singling out AI as a productivity lever that can improve public service delivery, accelerate scientific discovery, strengthen healthcare outcomes, and transform education. He also called for deepening the corporate bond market, pension and insurance funds, municipal finance and innovative infrastructure financing — the plumbing of a deeper capital market that a high-growth economy will need.

"The journey ahead is focused on capitalising on the emerging opportunities."

— Shaktikanta Das, principal secretary to the prime minister, at the Kautilya Economic Conclave

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, Das's remarks land in a week when the finance minister told the same conclave that India had weathered four years of global turbulence with its fundamentals intact. The message for NRI investors is consistent: the growth story is domestic-demand led, the external buffers (reserves near $766 billion, a services surplus, steady remittances) are intact, and the next leg of reform is about deepening capital markets — which directly affects the investment vehicles available to returning and remote investors. The 8% figure is not a forecast from the government; it is the target the reform architecture is being judged against.

What's next

The test of Das's thesis is whether the 7.8% June-quarter pace holds through the second half of FY27 as global headwinds — trade weaponization, energy volatility, and a US rate cycle in flux — press on emerging markets. The corporate bond market and AI-productivity agenda he outlined are the longer-horizon bets; the near-term data to watch is the September-quarter GDP print.
nri_angle: The domestic-demand growth story underpins the NRI investment case — steady remittances, services surplus and deepening capital markets keep the macro backdrop for diaspora portfolios supportive.
